name: english_01
context: An English tweet from the SemEval-2017 sentiment analysis dataset. The tweets were found by searching Twitter for popular topics of the time, such as public figures, products, places, events and political issues, and were posted between 2012 and early 2017. At least five crowd workers labelled the overall sentiment of each tweet.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 1 broke the 400-word limit, so this rewrite keeps its changes and cuts words. Version 0 under-predicted neutral (98/196). Mild grumbles, sports critique, corrections, waiting and missing out went to negative, though annotators call them neutral. Plans, invites, promos and mild hopes went to positive, also neutral for annotators. News headlines were mislabelled neutral even though annotators gave them the sentiment of the event: injury, violence or failure made them negative, and achievements or firsts made them positive. To fix this, positive and negative now need a clear feeling, and news takes the valence of a clearly good or bad event. To get under 400 words, I removed the long condolence and event-promo examples, shortened the rule and every criterion field, and moved condolences into the positive cues.
next_examples_not_copied: Imma need Brook Lopez to get more aggressive on the boards. 7 feet tall, c’mon son

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 1 overcorrected. Raising the bar for positive and negative pushed 82 positive and 69 negative texts into neutral, and macro-F1 fell from 69.8 to 66.2. These annotators label a tweet positive or negative whenever it leans either way, even mildly. Positive covers event promos with invitations ('come see me!!', 'Come enjoy Splash Dance'), looking forward to plans, wanting something ('I want IHOP tomorrow'), mild interest in products ('may be my next phone'), giveaways and RIP wishes. Negative covers small annoyances (':(', '#Fml', '#boring', 'can't make it'), delays, can't-go remarks and mild gripes. Neutral is for no lean at all. The texts that stayed neutral across both versions are of a few kinds. Sports commentary, scores and predictions about players or teams with no personal emotion. Argumentative replies and debates. Factual corrections and news about third parties without a clear outcome for the author's side. Version 2 therefore goes back to the version 0 approach, where mild lean counts. I add explicit neutral carve-outs for sports and game commentary, debating replies and impersonal news. Promos with invites or exclamation marks count as positive, and RIP and condolence wishes are positive. Examples come from both versions' errors.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 3 is the best so far (71.0). Its remaining errors fall into two main groups.

1) Positive texts labelled neutral (54). Many are inviting promos: 'Come enjoy Splash Dance', 'join us at Rum Runners', 'Invite all your friends', giveaways and chances to win. Others are reports of achievements or milestones: 'David Price's 100th career win!', 'walk-off', 'first and only artist to win', 'clear winner'. Many more are casual personal plans with a light upbeat tone. Version 3 told the model that promos and plans are neutral, which was too broad. It should separate invitations to enjoy something (positive) from plain ticket sales and listings (neutral).

2) Neutral texts labelled negative (42). These are mostly wry or joking remarks about one's own situation ('no one to go out with so i guess i'll be on netflix'), teasing jokes about celebrities, and opinion or argument about politics, religion or sport without insults. Neutral also covers corrections and heads-ups.

News of bad events (injury, violence) remains labelled neutral against gold negative. I will add a light pointer for clearly bad news and clearly good achievements, but news about game results is inconsistent in the data, so I won't push it far. I keep the version 3 structure and adjust these lines.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 4 scored 72.5, the best so far, with 164 errors. Its additions helped positive recall: inviting promos and achievements moved from 54 to 33 positive misses. But they also pushed more neutral texts into positive (28 to 45). Most of these are plain game reports ('Trayce Thompson's 2-run double gives the White Sox a 5-4 lead', 'Twins rally for 8-6 win', 'Dustin Johnson leads the PGA', 'Yanks crush Sox'). Others are 'who wants to go with me?' invitations to friends, hype for others' events, and nostalgia ('found my old ipod'). The annotators keep plain game results and leads neutral. Only celebrated personal milestones or records with clear excitement are positive.

Neutral texts labelled negative (29) are again mostly wry self-situations, opinion about politics or celebrities, and impersonal news of injuries or illness ('Everton boss... struggling with injuries', 'Ebola nurse may have been sick'). So the news clause should be limited to violence, deaths and scandals with clear victims, not routine injury or team news.

Negative texts labelled neutral (38) include small personal setbacks ('Sorry I can't make it', 'but i cant'), sarcastic jokes with a negative edge, and harsh-sounding comparisons. I add cues for can't-make-it and sarcastic exaggeration.

Version 5 keeps the version 4 structure. It adds plain scores and asking friends to come along as neutral, narrows the news clause, and adds can't-make-it cues for negative.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 5 scored 71.7, slightly below version 4's 72.5. Several neutral rules in version 5 pulled positive recall down from 158 to 144: plain game results, asking a friend along, and team or injury news. The gain on neutral-to-positive errors (45 to 34) did not make up for this. Negative recall rose from 156 to 166, helped by the can't-make-it and sarcasm cues, but more neutral texts were again labelled negative (29 to 41). Most of these are wry or joking self-remarks and pointed opinions on public figures. Version 5 had dropped version 4's distress qualifier on opinions and its teasing-celebrities clause, and moved wry self-jokes from the main criteria into the negative not_for.

The gold labels are noisy around these boundaries, so wholesale shifts mostly trade one error for another. Version 6 goes back to version 4 and keeps only the narrow gains from version 5:
- can't-make-it and 'but I can't' cues for negative;
- a short note, only in the positive not_for, that plain score updates are neutral. This should cut the most obvious game-report false positives without the broader neutral rules.
The 'come enjoy, join us' wording for public promos stays positive. Asking a single friend along gets no special rule. Opinion, teasing and wry self-joke texts stay neutral without insults or clear distress, as in version 4.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 7 went 6 words over the limit, so this rewrite keeps its one change and trims wording. That change keeps version 6 and adds voting or retweet appeals and 'who wants to go with me?' to the neutral cues and the positive not_for, with a mention of voting or retweet appeals in the rule. To get under 400 words, I shortened the rule's last two sentences, dropped 'plain plans' from the positive not_for, and cut 'still waiting' and 'should' from the neutral cues. The labelling logic is otherwise the same as version 6.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 7 is the best so far (73.8). This version makes one narrow change and leaves the rest alone, because the remaining errors are mostly label noise.

The largest coherent group of neutral texts labelled negative is plain news about arrests, trials, executions, illness or crime that the author does not comment on:
- 'SC says Yakub can be executed on Thursday'
- 'Ebola nurse may have been sick before taking the plane'
- 'Bahrain regime's arrest of Nabeel Rajab'
- 'Boko Haram... may have benefitted from money gotten from crude oil theft'

Annotators labelled these neutral. Reports of violence, deaths and injuries ('shot dead', the Gavin Henson injury) were labelled negative. So the rule now marks plain reports of arrests, trials, illness or crime as neutral, keeps violence and injury news negative, and drops 'scandal'.

To stay under 400 words, I removed 'invite your friends' and 'chance to win' from the positive cues and 'may' from the neutral cues. Everything else stays the same.

versions.analysis_for_next: Versions 7 and 8 both score 73.8, so the prompt has plateaued and the remaining errors are mostly label noise. One fixable group remains: about six neutral game reports labelled positive, such as 'Twins rally for 8-6 win', 'Yanks crush Sox', 'Dustin Johnson leads the PGA Championship', 'Arsenal have won three PL games...' and 'Trayce Thompson's 2-run double...'. The rule's phrase 'wins of note' probably invites this. Annotators gave positive to milestones, records and firsts ('100th career win!', 'first and only artist to win'), not to ordinary game results. So I replace 'achievements, milestones or wins of note' with 'milestones, records or firsts' in the rule and in the positive 'what', and add 'game results' to the positive not_for. Everything else, including version 8's neutral treatment of plain arrest, trial and illness reports, stays the same.

versions.analysis_for_next: Versions 7, 8 and 9 all score 73.8 macro-F1, with errors spread evenly. Swapping 'wins of note' for 'milestones, records or firsts' fixed a few game-result false positives, but about as many positive texts moved to neutral, so the net change was zero. What remains is mostly label noise. Near-identical texts carry different gold labels: missing a TV show is negative once (#boring) and neutral once ('Wth am i supposed to do...'). Personal plans to see a concert are sometimes positive and sometimes neutral. Plain news of arrests is neutral, while injuries or violence are negative. Earlier attempts to move any of these boundaries as a whole (versions 1, 2 and 5) lowered the score by trading one error type for another. For the final version I keep version 9 unchanged, since it is as accurate as the best versions and states the narrowest, best-supported distinctions.
